summary: The Monitor Accountability Act directs the Judicial Conference to issue rules capping fees, limiting monitors to one five-year term at a time with no reappointment or same-employer succession, requiring public comment before appointment, annual public fee-and-service accountings, hearings before any revision, and automatic transfer of any monitorship case to a new judge after six years, with retroactive application to existing long-term monitorships.

scores.thoughts: The bill imposes limits on fees that court-appointed monitors may charge (capping rates, allowing pro bono/reduced rates, requiring annual public accounting of fees). Monitors are typically paid by the state or local government subject to the monitorship. These provisions would modestly constrain or reduce such expenditures.
The bill contains no provisions related to taxes, tax rates, or revenue collection.
The bill contains no provisions related to healthcare policy, coverage, or regulation.
The bill contains no provisions related to firearms or gun regulations.
The bill contains no provisions related to immigration, borders, or pathways to citizenship.
The bill contains no provisions related to abortion access or restrictions.
The bill contains no provisions related to military or defense spending.

The bill contains no provisions related to welfare programs or social safety-net benefits.
The bill contains no provisions related to schools, education funding, or school choice.
The bill contains no provisions related to drug enforcement or decriminalization.

The bill addresses procedural rules for court monitors that could arise in various civil cases (including some policing or justice-related consent decrees), but it does not alter sentencing, policing practices, or criminal-justice policy itself.
The bill contains no provisions related to trade, tariffs, or globalization.
